drills.q: What range must an array's values fall into for cyclic sort to be applicable at all?
drills.a: A known, contiguous range tied to the array's own length, e.g. [1,n], [0,n-1], or [0,n]. Without that constraint the technique simply doesn't apply.

drills.q: For an array with values in [1,n], what index is the 'home' for value v, and what mistake results from off-by-one confusion here?
drills.a: Home index is v - 1. Using v directly (as if 0-indexed range) causes an off-by-one shift in every placement, or an out-of-bounds access when v equals n.

drills.q: Prove that cyclic sort's nested while loop is actually O(n) total work, not O(n^2).
drills.a: Every executed swap places exactly one value into its permanent, correct home index, and once a value is at its home it is never touched again (the loop only advances past an index once the value there is confirmed correct). Since there are only n values total, the number of swaps across the algorithm's entire execution -- summed over every outer iteration -- cannot exceed n. Combined with the O(n) outer advances, total work is O(n).

drills.q: A candidate's cyclic sort implementation infinite-loops on input [1, 1, 3]. What's the likely bug?
drills.a: Missing the swap guard nums[i] != nums[correctIndex]. With duplicate value 1 present, once index 0 holds a 1 and index 0 IS the home for value 1, the code should advance i -- but if it swaps unconditionally whenever nums[i] != i+1 without checking whether the target slot already holds the same value, it can swap the same pair back and forth indefinitely.

drills.q: Design the negative-marking approach for Find All Duplicates in an Array (LC442), and state precisely when you record a value as a duplicate.
drills.a: For each value v in the array (in original left-to-right order), compute idx = abs(v) - 1. If nums[idx] is already negative, then abs(v) has been seen before -- record it as a duplicate before (re-)negating nums[idx]. If nums[idx] is positive, negate it to mark abs(v) as seen for the first time. Using abs(v) rather than v is required because v itself may have already been negated by an earlier iteration.

drills.q: Explain why First Missing Positive (LC41) must ignore any nums[i] that is <= 0 or > n during the placement pass, rather than trying to place it somewhere.
drills.a: The array has length n, so there are only n valid home slots (for values 1..n). A value outside [1,n] has no valid home index in this array and can never itself be the answer, since the first missing positive for any length-n array is guaranteed (by pigeonhole) to lie in [1, n+1]. Attempting to compute a home index for an out-of-range value produces a negative or out-of-bounds index, which either crashes or, if silently wrapped/clamped, corrupts an unrelated slot's data.

drills.q: A problem states the input array for Find the Duplicate Number cannot be modified. Can you still use cyclic sort? If not, what do you use instead and why does it not need mutation?
drills.a: No -- cyclic sort requires swapping elements in place, which mutates the array, violating the constraint. Instead, treat nums[i] as a pointer to the next index (an implicit linked list, since values are constrained to [1,n] and the array has n+1 elements, guaranteeing a cycle by pigeonhole) and run Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection, which only ever reads array values and moves pointer variables -- it never writes to the array. Alternatively, binary search over the value range [1,n], counting how many array elements are <= mid at each step, also avoids mutation at the cost of O(n log n) instead of O(n).

drills.q: Solve Set Mismatch (LC645) using pure arithmetic (no array mutation, no extra space beyond a few scalars), and state the two equations you need.
drills.a: Let d = the duplicate value, m = the missing value. From sum(nums) - sum(1..n) = d - m (the duplicate contributes twice, the missing contributes zero, everything else cancels), and sum(nums^2) - sum((1..n)^2) = d^2 - m^2 = (d-m)(d+m). Divide the second equation by the first (d - m) to get (d+m), then combine with (d-m) to solve for both d and m via simple addition/subtraction. Watch for integer overflow on the squared sums when n is large in fixed-width-integer languages.
